rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Three calcium compounds, three hydration stories. **Quick lime (CaO)** is born from limestone calcination (CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂, ~1000 °C) and slakes violently (CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + heat), fluxes silica to CaSiO₃ in the furnace, and yields calcium carbide with coke at 2000 °C.…

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***The hospital cast*** — a bandage soaked in plaster-of-Paris slurry is wrapped on the fracture; within minutes the hemihydrate drinks 1½ H₂O, grows interlocking gypsum needles, and the soft wrap becomes a rigid cast — setting chemistry holding a bone straight.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Quick Lime, Bleaching Powder, Plaster of Paris, Magnesia, Epsom Salt Three calcium compounds and two magnesium ones carry most of the unit's industrial chemistry: **CaO** (quick lime) — made by calcining limestone and slaked to Ca(OH)₂; **bleaching powder** Ca(OCl)Cl — chlorine absorbed in slaked lime; **plaster of Paris** CaSO₄·½H₂O — gypsum dehydrated at ~120 °C; **magnesia** MgO — from…  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 Calcium oxide (quick lime) - **Preparation:** calcination of limestone in a lime kiln ~1000 °C: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂↑ (reversible; CO₂ swept out). - White amorphous solid, mp ~2600 °C; reacts violently with water (**slaking**): CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + heat — the slaked lime. - With acids: CaO + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O. With CO₂ (slowly) back to carbonate.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: 120 C for PoP (not 200 -> dead-burnt). Available chlorine 35-38%. Bleaching agent = HOCl -> [O]. Slaking = CaO + H2O exothermic. Carbide: CaO + 3C -> CaC2 + CO.

Write its reaction with dilute sulphuric acid and give two uses.** — Bleaching powder is made by passing **dry chlorine over slaked lime**: Ca(OH)₂ + Cl₂ → Ca(OCl)Cl + H₂O — industrially in the **Hasenclever plant**, where chlorine is fed upward through a series of rotating drums…  ·  **NEB-style (2m): How is plaster of Paris prepared? Why should gypsum not be heated above about 200 °C?** — Plaster of Paris (calcium sulphate hemihydrate, CaSO₄·½H₂O) is prepared by **heating gypsum, CaSO₄·2H₂O, at about 120 °C**: CaSO₄·2H₂O → CaSO₄·½H₂O + 1½H₂O.…

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: All three compounds are hydration stories: CaO's slaking is hydration releasing heat, plaster's setting is re-hydration interlocking crystals, and bleaching powder's decay is hydration-triggered hydrolysis — store all three away from water or vapour.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Quick lime CaO: limestone calcination ~1000 C (CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2, reversible, sweep CO2); violent slaking CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2 + heat; with SiO2 -> CaSiO3 (flux); with coke 2000 C -> CaC2 + CO; drying agent (not for NH3); uses cement/flux/carbide.…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Cement clinker is mostly calcium silicates — every tonne of Portland cement begins with ~1.2 t of limestone calcined exactly as the quick-lime equation, making CaCO₃ decomposition the single largest industrial CO₂ source.

Above ~200 °C the remaining water is driven out entirely: anhydrite ("dead-burnt plaster") has no such channels, hydrates too slowly to set, and the plaster is useless.…  ·  ## 5. rows.text: Write equations for quick lime with water, silica and coke, naming each product and use.  ·  ## 6. Common Confusions **Plaster of Paris is a hemihydrate, not a hydrate:** the formula is CaSO₄·½H₂O — half a mole of water per mole of salt; writing CaSO₄·H₂O loses the mark.  ·  **Bleaching powder bleaches by oxygen, not by chlorine alone:** the active agent is HOCl → HCl + [O]; the chlorine is the carrier.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Quick lime is not slaked lime:** CaO vs Ca(OH)₂ — slaking converts one to the other; bleaching powder needs the *slaked* lime.  ·  **Milk of magnesia is a suspension, not a solution:** the antacid is Mg(OH)₂, which is almost insoluble — its mildness (weak base, low solubility) is exactly why it neutralises stomach acid without the causticity of NaOH.  ·  ## 7.
